content_voiceover: This final initiation slide completes the amplification story by adding factor eleven. On the right, thrombin generated at the bottom feeds back to activate platelets and factor eleven, shown in the blue oval labeled activated platelets and factor eleven, converting it to factor eleven a. Factor eleven a then activates additional factor nine into factor nine a, supplementing the factor nine a already produced by the extrinsic tenase. This gives the system two independent sources of factor nine a, extrinsic tenase and factor eleven a, both feeding the intrinsic tenase complex above. This redundancy massively amplifies thrombin generation and helps explain why deficiencies of factor eleven, or of the contact pathway components upstream of it, can produce clinically significant bleeding despite an intact extrinsic pathway. This whole network of feedback loops, thrombin activating factors five, eight, and eleven, is what produces the sharp thrombin burst seen in the propagation phase of the curve.
keypoints: Thrombin activates platelets and factor eleven, generating factor eleven a
Factor eleven a provides a second source of factor nine a
This creates redundant amplification feeding the intrinsic tenase
Explains why factor eleven deficiency can cause clinically relevant bleeding
keypoint_voiceover: Factor eleven a is thrombin's second amplification tool, it makes more factor nine a to feed intrinsic tenase alongside the extrinsic tenase. That redundancy is why factor eleven deficiency, though variable, can still cause real bleeding on boards questions.
